title: Communion and the sending
hookLine: Catholics receive; others often come forward for a blessing; then go forth, the Mass is ended

lines: ROW BY ROW, A SLOW LINE.
cards: Row by row, people stand and walk up the aisle in a slow line. An old woman with a walker. A dad carrying a sleeping toddler.
A teenager in a hoodie. At the front, a priest or a lay minister holds up a small white host to each person and says four words: the Body of Christ. Each one answers with one word: Amen.
Mixed into the line are people who aren't receiving. They come up with their arms crossed over their chest, and the minister gives them a blessing instead. Nobody stares.

teach.b: Communion means union, sharing together. Catholics believe they receive Christ himself, so they prepare: at peace with God, having gone to confession for any serious sin, and fasting from food for an hour before.
They receive on the tongue or in the hand, and sometimes from the cup too.

That Amen is a whole creed in one word: yes, this is Christ, and yes, I belong to his body, the Church. Saint Augustine told new Christians something like: receive what you are, and become what you receive.
Because communion is a sign of full unity in the Church, Catholics usually ask others not to receive. It isn't meant as a judgment on anyone.

teach.h: A BLESSING FOR THOSE NOT RECEIVING.
teach.b: So in many parishes, anyone may come forward with arms crossed for a blessing. Afterward: silence, a last prayer, a blessing. Then the deacon or priest sends everyone out.
In the old Latin: Ite, missa est. Go, it is the sending. Missa became Mass, today's word.
Christians have gathered for it every Sunday for nearly two thousand years, and for about sixteen hundred of them it has carried the name of its last line: you're being sent.

Look back over these two weeks: the entrance, through my fault, Lord have mercy, the Gloria, the readings, the Gospel and the homily, the creed and the prayers, the gifts carried up, holy, holy, holy, the consecration, the Great Amen and the Our Father, the Lamb of God, and now communion and the sending.
The Mass doesn't end at the door. It's aimed at it.

how: Catholics who are prepared come forward to receive communion, answering Amen to 'the Body of Christ'; in many parishes those not receiving come forward with arms crossed for a blessing; after a closing prayer and blessing, the deacon or priest dismisses the people.

o: the Catholic word for any church building
from a Latin word for a gathered crowd
named for the Latin words that send people out

games.q: what's inside the end of Mass — tap the pairs.

s: the word Mass comes from the moment of the sending
Ite, missa est: go, it is the sending. missa became Mass.
anyone at Mass is expected to receive communion
communion is a sign of full unity in the Church, so Catholics usually ask others not to receive. many come up for a blessing.
Catholics fast for a while before receiving
from food for an hour before communion.

games.q: you're visiting a Catholic Mass with a friend. you're not Catholic. the communion line reaches your row. what do many parishes invite you to do?
o: come forward with arms crossed for a blessing.
games.why: many parishes invite anyone to come forward with arms crossed over the chest and receive a blessing. staying seated is fine too.

practice: Picture walking out a door into the rest of your day, and ask: where am I being sent? Pick one person and one kind thing you could do for them before tonight, a text, a favor, a patient answer, and be specific.
If you pray, ask to be sent well; if not, just make it your mission for the day.

wordCard.voice: Mass. From the Latin missa, the sending: the whole Catholic liturgy, named for the moment the people are sent out. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: go, it is the sending (the dismissal). missa gave the whole liturgy its name.

carryVoice: Your line: the Mass is a sending. That closes the walk through the Mass; tomorrow, the rosary. That's day one hundred seventeen.
